what: How a former 'street kid' is key to South Africa's police corruption inquiry

clean_source_blocks.text: Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala, due to appear at the Madlanga Commission, grew up hustling to make a living.

Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala addressed some of the accusations against him when he spoke to lawmakers about corruption in the police force last year Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala's name has haunted the proceedings of South Africa's major inquiry into alleged police corruption and, if things go to plan on Wednesday, the controversial businessman will at last be questioned himself. He has been accused of supplying generous gifts - including 20 impalas, the weight-loss drug Ozempic and personal loans - to help him buy influence and get police contracts. The 49-year-old, who has been in police custody for more than a year in connection with a separate case, is expected to get the chance to provide his side of the story as he comes before retired Constitutional Court judge Mbuyiseli Madlanga and his panel.

The magistrate at the Pretoria court is expected to give his ruling on the plea deal next week. Matlala, who is also facing a separate murder charge that he denies, has been named by a witness at the corruption inquiry known as the Madlanga Commission as being part of a drug-trafficking cartel that has managed to penetrate the police. He has not commented on this accusation but, giving evidence at a parallel parliamentary corruption inquiry last year, denied knowing senior police officers and politicians personally. Matlala has yet to appear at the Madlanga Commission. Witnesses at that inquiry, which began last September, have alleged collusion between criminal underworld figures and senior police officials. It was set up after senior police officer Lt-Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged last July that organised crime groups had infiltrated the government. 'Gifts' from a lover

The revelations at the Madlanga Commission, in progress for 10 months, have gripped South Africans and they are eager to hear how Matlala responds. Dressed in a Fendi shirt and Gucci glasses, Matlala did give evidence at a parallel corruption inquiry in parliament last November. He said he did not know senior police officers and politicians personally and denied corruption allegations though he admitted to having made donations for activities related to the African National Congress (ANC), the main party in the coalition government. But he has not yet been asked to address the wider allegations made at the Madlanga Commission or the accusation that he was part of a drug trafficking cartel, allegedly known as the Big Five. "Cat" Matlala and his wife Tsakane Matlala deny an attempted murder charge

[Lähde: AOL | URL: https://www.aol.com/articles/key-figure-south-africa-police-124923000.html]
Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala, a central figure in a major ongoing police graft inquiry in South Africa, has pleaded guilty to corruption, fraud and money-laundering charges as part of a deal with state prosecutors.

He was accused of bribing top police officials to win a 360m rand ($22m; £16.5m) tender for his health company Medicare24 in 2024.

The plea deal, which has not yet been accepted by the magistrate, would result in Matlala giving evidence against "high-ranking officials", state advocate Santhos Manilall said.

Police chief Gen Fannie Masemola is one of those facing charges in relation to this case. He has denied the charges.

Manilall told the court in the capital, Pretoria, that it had taken almost two months of negotiations to put the deal together.

If accepted, it would result in Matlala, 49, serving eight years in prison.

The state's lawyer said that the "sacrifice" of a more lenient sentence would be worth it, as "for the first time we have an accused who has... given us detail that we would not have been made aware of".

As part of the deal, Matlala is required to give honest and frank testimony at future trials.

But in a blistering attack, the Democratic Alliance (DA), the junior partner in South Africa's governing coalition, called the arrangement a "sweetheart deal" and "a betrayal of accountability" that may not result in a successful prosecution.

DA justice spokesperson Glynnis Breytenbach said it was evidence of a two-tier justice system, as "one of the country's most prominent corruption accused is allowed to negotiate what amounts to a discounted sentence".

The magistrate at the Pretoria court is expected to give his ruling on the plea deal next week.

Matlala, who is also facing a separate murder charge that he denies, has been named by a witness at the corruption inquiry known as the Madlanga Commission as being part of a drug-trafficking cartel that has managed to penetrate the police.

He has not commented on this accusation but, giving evidence at a parallel parliamentary corruption inquiry last year, denied knowing senior police officers and politicians personally.

Matlala has yet to appear at the Madlanga Commission.

Witnesses at that inquiry, which began last September, have alleged collusion between criminal underworld figures and senior police officials.

It was set up after senior police officer Lt-Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged last July that organised crime groups had infiltrated the government.

payload.title: Vusimusi Matlalaa odotetaan kuultavaksi Etelä-Afrikan poliisikorruptiosta
payload.summary: Liikemies Vusimusi ”Cat” Matlalan odotetaan vastaavan Madlanga-komissiossa väitteisiin vaikutusvallan ostamisesta ja yhteyksistä poliisiin soluttautuneeseen rikollisuuteen.
payload.content:
Etelä-Afrikan poliisin väitettyä korruptiota tutkivan Madlanga-komission huomio kohdistuu keskiviikkona liikemies Vusimusi ”Cat” Matlalaan. Komission kuulemisissa usein mainitun 49-vuotiaan Matlalan odotetaan vastaavan itse väitteisiin, joiden mukaan hän hankki lahjoilla vaikutusvaltaa, tavoitteli poliisisopimuksia ja kuului poliisiin soluttautuneeseen rikollisverkostoon.

## Lahjoja ja rikollisyhteyksiä koskevat väitteet

Matlalan väitetään käyttäneen anteliaita lahjoja vaikutusvallan hankkimiseen ja poliisin sopimusten saamiseen. Väitteissä luetellaan 20 impalaa, Ozempic-laihdutuslääkettä ja henkilökohtaisia lainoja. Matlalan nimi on ollut esillä koko suuren korruptiotutkinnan ajan, mutta hän ei ole tähän mennessä saanut Madlanga-komissiossa tilaisuutta vastata näihin laajempiin syytöksiin.

Komission kuulema todistaja on lisäksi nimennyt Matlalan osaksi Big Five -nimellä tunnettua huumekauppakartellia, jonka väitetään päässeen poliisin sisälle. Matlala ei ole kommentoinut tätä väitettä. Hän on ollut yli vuoden poliisin säilössä erillisen tapauksen yhteydessä. Hän kiistää erillisen murhasyytteen, ja Matlala sekä hänen vaimonsa Tsakane Matlala ovat kiistäneet myös murhayrityssyytteen. Pretorian tuomioistuimen odotetaan antavan ensi viikolla ratkaisunsa syyteneuvottelusta.

Ennen liikemieheksi nousuaan Matlala hankki nuorena elantoaan kadulla. Madlanga-komission rinnalla toimivan parlamentaarisen korruptiotutkinnan kuulemisessa viime marraskuussa hän esiintyi Fendi-paidassa ja Gucci-laseissa. Matlala kiisti tuolloin korruptioväitteet ja sanoi, ettei tunne henkilökohtaisesti korkeita poliisivirkailijoita tai poliitikkoja. Hän kuitenkin myönsi tehneensä lahjoituksia Afrikan kansalliskongressiin eli ANC:hen liittyvään toimintaan. ANC on hallituskoalition pääpuolue.

## Komissio tutkii poliisin ja rikollispiirien yhteyksiä

Madlanga-komissio aloitti työnsä viime syyskuussa, ja tutkinta on jatkunut noin kymmenen kuukautta. Se perustettiin sen jälkeen, kun kenraaliluutnantti Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi väitti viime heinäkuussa järjestäytyneiden rikollisryhmien soluttautuneen valtionhallintoon. Kuulemisissa todistajat ovat esittäneet väitteitä rikollisen alamaailman toimijoiden ja poliisin ylimpien virkamiesten yhteistyöstä. Paljastukset ovat herättäneet Etelä-Afrikassa laajaa huomiota.

Komissiota johtaa eläkkeellä oleva perustuslakituomioistuimen tuomari Mbuyiseli Madlanga yhdessä paneelinsa kanssa. Jos keskiviikolle suunniteltu kuuleminen toteutuu, Matlala saa ensimmäisen kerran vastata suoraan komissiolle paitsi lahjoja ja poliisisopimuksia koskeviin väitteisiin myös väitettyyn Big Five -yhteyteensä. Hänen odotetaan esittävän oman kantansa tutkinnassa, jossa hänen nimensä on noussut esiin toistuvasti.
summary_bullets: Vusimusi Matlalan odotetaan saapuvan Madlanga-komission kuultavaksi keskiviikkona.
Häntä koskevat väitteet liittyvät lahjoihin, poliisisopimuksiin ja järjestäytyneeseen rikollisuuteen.
Matlala on aiemmin kiistänyt korruptioväitteet parlamentaarisessa kuulemisessa.
payload.journalist_note: Korruptio- ja rikollisuusyhteyksiä koskevat tiedot on ilmaistu todistajien esittäminä väitteinä. Matlalan aiemmat kiistot sekä väitteet, joita hän ei ole kommentoinut, on erotettu toisistaan.

Hänen odotetaan esittävän oman kantansa tutkinnassa, jossa hänen nimensä on noussut esiin toistuvasti.

article.source_text:
Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala, due to appear at the Madlanga Commission, grew up hustling to make a living.

Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala addressed some of the accusations against him when he spoke to lawmakers about corruption in the police force last year Vusimusi "Cat" Matlala's name has haunted the proceedings of South Africa's major inquiry into alleged police corruption and, if things go to plan on Wednesday, the controversial businessman will at last be questioned himself. He has been accused of supplying generous gifts - including 20 impalas, the weight-loss drug Ozempic and personal loans - to help him buy influence and get police contracts. The 49-year-old, who has been in police custody for more than a year in connection with a separate case, is expected to get the chance to provide his side of the story as he comes before retired Constitutional Court judge Mbuyiseli Madlanga and his panel.

The magistrate at the Pretoria court is expected to give his ruling on the plea deal next week. Matlala, who is also facing a separate murder charge that he denies, has been named by a witness at the corruption inquiry known as the Madlanga Commission as being part of a drug-trafficking cartel that has managed to penetrate the police. He has not commented on this accusation but, giving evidence at a parallel parliamentary corruption inquiry last year, denied knowing senior police officers and politicians personally. Matlala has yet to appear at the Madlanga Commission. Witnesses at that inquiry, which began last September, have alleged collusion between criminal underworld figures and senior police officials. It was set up after senior police officer Lt-Gen Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi alleged last July that organised crime groups had infiltrated the government. 'Gifts' from a lover

The revelations at the Madlanga Commission, in progress for 10 months, have gripped South Africans and they are eager to hear how Matlala responds. Dressed in a Fendi shirt and Gucci glasses, Matlala did give evidence at a parallel corruption inquiry in parliament last November. He said he did not know senior police officers and politicians personally and denied corruption allegations though he admitted to having made donations for activities related to the African National Congress (ANC), the main party in the coalition government. But he has not yet been asked to address the wider allegations made at the Madlanga Commission or the accusation that he was part of a drug trafficking cartel, allegedly known as the Big Five.
